as_told.title: Marconi's transatlantic signal bounced off the ionosphere

plain: The radio pioneer Guglielmo Marconi's first signal across the Atlantic, sent between Newfoundland and Cornwall in 1901, worked almost by luck: his radio waves bounced off the ionosphere, a layer of charged gas high in the atmosphere, and came back down to the receiver, just as the physicist James Clerk Maxwell's theory of electromagnetic waves allowed. That is how a scientist named Filippo Biondi, who scans beneath the pyramids with radar, explains it, without naming a source. Michels later passes the story on from Biondi, calling Marconi ignorant in a useful way, someone who simply tried it across the ocean when others would not have bothered.
